en: The Śramaṇa Zhànruán of Pílíng during the Táng dynasty composed this work.
As for the citation of analogies, both the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* rely on the analogy of a tree to represent the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma);

therefore, they are called "the Tree of the Path. These two treatises are largely identical to the present text, with the sole exception that the latter pertains to the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*).
Regarding the first stage (prathamabhūmi),
it differs from the *Vibhāṣā*.
Within this, there are further two [subdivisions].

First, there is a separate treatment concerning the unconditioned path-factors (*asaṃskṛta-mārga-pakṣya*); next, there is a general treatment concerning the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).
The initial passage contains a simile, its application, and a conclusion.
The analogies and the corresponding textual passages are both missing the "as one wishes" (yathā-icchā) element.
Within the analogy, it should state that the trunk rises upward, which corresponds to the "basis of psychic power as one wishes" (ṛddhipāda).
This is the downward application to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
First, the formal correspondence is established.
Next, the various names for the fruition are clarified.
Under the section on the factors of enlightenment and spiritual friends, the preceding correspondence with the analogy is concluded.
Within the preparatory means, there are three types of spiritual friends who guide one from the beginning until reaching the place of treasure;
these are the "companions on the journey."
By means of these factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa), one acts without error;
this is the meaning of instruction.
Through these various factors, one guards against and prevents the intrusion of delusions and errors.
This refers to the meaning of external protection:
taking patience as one's robe and the joy of the Dharma as one's food,
thereby sustaining the life of wisdom and augmenting the body of meditative concentration.
And it explains the meaning of external protection.
By means of the three types of knowledge,
one is led to enter the first dwelling of the perfect awakening of the three bodies.
This can serve as a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) for sentient beings.
Generally speaking, the lower [teachings] are categorized according to the three truths (trisatya);
whereas previously, they were only categorized according to the specific stages of the Perfect (yuan) and Distinct (bie) teachings.
This is explained generally by distinguishing each individual truth (*satya*).
Within this, first there is the specific correspondence,
followed by the general correspondence.
The two pairs of general and specific [categories] are merely employed as metaphors in the text;
they do not pertain to the stages of cultivation.
Furthermore, regarding the analogy for the Perfect [Teaching] based on the vertical sequence of stages:
Contemplation of conduct is the leaf;
semblance [attainment] is the flower;
and partial realization of truth is the fruit.
If one were to explain this by applying it generally across the four teachings, it can be understood accordingly.
Next, in clarifying the three gates of liberation, one elucidates the functional efficacy of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Chapter 21, asks:
"Since Nirvāṇa has but a single gate, why are there three? The answer is as follows:
The Dharma is one, while its meanings are three;
yet these three are in fact one.
Furthermore, they are distinguished as three according to the differences among individuals.
Those whose conduct is dominated by views proceed from emptiness;
those whose conduct is dominated by craving proceed from wishlessness;
and those for whom views and craving are equal proceed from signlessness.
While this treatise was originally restricted to the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka), it now extends across the three teachings.
This is because the initial stage of the Distinct Teaching (Bie-jiao) is identical to that of the two [lesser] teachings.
All teachings alike take the path of realization as the city of the outflow-free (anāsrava).
Only the meaning of "perfect" (yuan) is universally applicable;
the six stages of "identity" (ji) distinguish the differences.
Therefore, the explanation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) in this text is now concluded.
Next, the three liberations are explained.
According to the literal meaning and the correct intent of the text,
one should explain only the three liberations of non-action (anabhisaṃskāra).
Furthermore, this serves to provide a comparative determination so that one may recognize non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
Therefore, the three liberations (*vimokṣa*) are clearly elucidated across all the teachings;
herein, first, the purpose for their introduction and their enumeration of names are clarified.
In the subsequent formal explanation, there is first a general exposition,

followed by a detailed analysis according to the various teachings. In the initial section, one first distinguishes between kings and ministers, the peripheral and the primary, and the distant and the proximate.
Next, [the stages] are categorized according to subduing and severing; thirdly, they are categorized according to name and essence,
using the general to encompass the specific.
The various teachings each differ regarding these three meanings;
according to the sacred scriptures, one cannot be exclusive to a single interpretation.
Therefore, [the texts] all state "or."
The following is an explanation according to the classification of teachings (yōkyō). I have merely provided notes here and there and will not analyze them separately;
one should instead derive their specific characteristics by following each respective teaching.
Regarding the initial section on the king and his ministers, it first clarifies that samādhi is the king,
followed by clarifying that the three liberations (vimokṣa) are the king.
The three liberations arise from wisdom, and samādhi arises from meditative concentration (samāpatti).
Regarding the establishment of two names for emptiness and so forth:
because two types of persons enter the untainted state differently,
there are differences between samādhi and the three liberations.
Those who personally enter the untainted state are the kings;
those who provide auxiliary support for its arising are the ministers.
Vision and reflection belong to wisdom (*prajñā*).
This means that concentration arises from wisdom;
by analogy, it should be understood that wisdom arises from concentration.
The definitions and essential natures of abandonment (*prahāṇa*) and suppression (*vibhava*) can be seen by consulting the text.
Next, regarding the sequential survey of the teachings:
the first three collections (Tripitaka) of the teachings are divided into three categories based on the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths;
this is the case in all the texts of the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*.
However, as for the mutual relationship between the three samādhis and the three liberations—
acting as king and minister—
this has not been clarified in the various treatises.
Therefore, within the Tripiṭaka, by contemplating this practice,
the higher patience (kṣānti) gives rise to the truth;
thus, this practice is established as the three gates.
Furthermore, these modes of practice merely adopt those that are similar in category to the three gates and are thus classified as belonging to the gates.
In the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), one contemplates from the very beginning that all things are like illusions;
therefore, one does not again rely upon the sixteen aspects of contemplation.
However, the three characteristics are distinguished by means of the contemplation of emptiness alone;
furthermore, the sovereign and the minister are distinguished by means of both meditative concentration and wisdom.
Although the three meanings, such as emptiness, all contemplate illusion, [they differ in their application].
It is not without reason that there is a distinction between kings and ministers;
this is likewise due to the differences in their faculties for entering the Path.
In the initial section on the Gate of Emptiness, I have fully cited the various commentaries and original texts from both ancient and modern times.
Since these two teachings differ in their respective ancient and modern presentations,
I now cite both to demonstrate the distinction between the provisional and the real.
These three gates in this teaching differ from the three gates of the Tripiṭaka, as their essential natures (svabhāva) are distinct.
In this context, attaining emptiness is itself signlessness and wishlessness.
Next, the distinct teaching is explained: first, it is generally presented in terms of the three contemplations;
next, it is specifically presented in terms of emerging into the provisional.
The meaning of the initial passage is that the three contemplations are themselves the three samādhis,
and the three liberations are likewise so.
Within each of the Truths (satya), cessation is samādhi and contemplation is the three liberations (vimokṣa).
Regarding the subduing and severing of kings and ministers, this follows the explanation in the Tripiṭaka.
One takes the first stage (*bhūmi*) as the city of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
Next, regarding those who emerge into the provisional (*prajñapti*),
since this single truth is established in meaning as threefold, [the following applies].
One should know that it also possesses the significance of both king and minister.
Regarding the establishment of two interpretations within the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao),
although the three truths (san-di) are present throughout the beginning and end of the teaching, [the distinction is made as follows].
Those who have not grasped the essential meaning rely solely on the provisional;
therefore, this teaching must be interpreted in two ways.
Furthermore, although a single teaching possesses the three truths from beginning to end, [the specific emphasis may vary].
If one enters the realization of the Way, it is no longer called "distinct";
therefore, the distinct teaching (biejiao) pertains only to the provisional.
All explanations of the meaning of the distinct [teaching] should be based on this principle.
Since the provisional emergence [of the bodhisattva] has already been explained through the three gates,
it also serves as the path leading toward the city of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Thus, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says:
To deliver sentient beings, one cultivates emptiness;
to protect and uphold all dharmas, one cultivates signlessness;
and without abandoning the realms of existence, one cultivates wishlessness.
Is it not the case that these three gates are established purely for the purpose of emerging into the provisional?
If even the emergence into the provisional is thus,
what need is there to seek further meaning in the other two gates, which spontaneously possess [that same quality]?
Next, regarding the explanation of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao):
whereas the preceding explanations of the three teachings were given directly,
the current explanation of the Perfect Teaching is said to be "distinctly categorized" (*bieyue*).
One should know that the first three [categories] are listed in a general, common manner;
since the primary intent of this text lies specifically in the Perfect [Teaching], its three gates of the Perfect are fundamentally different from the former.
Furthermore, the relationship between the Perfect King and his ministers is likewise utterly distinct.
Therefore, in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), emptiness is itself signlessness and non-action.
While the phrasing may resemble that of Daoism, the underlying meaning is fundamentally and eternally divergent.
In this teaching, concentration and wisdom are one in essence, and there is both perfect subduing and perfect severance.
The two meanings of "perfect" (*yuan*) and "wondrous essence" (*miaoti*) are mutually integrated.
Within this, first, I shall cite the treatise to provide a general comparative determination;
second, I shall provide the formal explanation.
Regarding the initial comparison and determination:
the objects of focus differ and the gates through which they are accessed vary.
The object of focus is precisely the untainted state of the first dwelling.
Therefore, it is made possible that the capacity to penetrate near and far also differs.
Regarding the phrase "the wise are equal," this clarifies that the essence of emptiness is not uniform.
The words of the wise also encompass the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) and the Teaching that Connects (Jie-tong).
Now, they reside solely in the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao), where the three liberations are perfected;
therein, emptiness is itself non-emptiness, and all are able to reach the ultimate.
Therefore, both are called "intermediate" and are both capable of seeing the nature.
Furthermore, the emptiness that is seen is empty and devoid of size;
it is only because of differences in cognition that the designations of "large" and "small" arise.
Therefore, herein, emptiness is defined by means of wisdom.
Since wisdom is already perfectly interfused, the two kinds of emptiness are unified.
Because they are unified, it is called the Middle Way, and one is further able to perceive the nature.
Furthermore, following the discussion of the inferior causes of the two vehicles, the distinctions between the eighteen emptinesses of the Great and Small Vehicles are explained.
Since one who attains this emptiness necessarily possesses all eighteen,
the eighteen emptinesses are discussed next.
If emptiness were not distinct from other gates,
then why would the two vehicles contemplate the eighteen kinds of emptiness as they would contemplate the events of a dream?
Now, regarding the eighteen great emptinesses below the Perfect [Teaching]:
when a person of the Perfect [Teaching] contemplates them, it is like contemplating the dharma of sleep;
the dharmas are like ignorance, and the dream-events are like grasping at marks.
Grasping at signs is a branch and a derivative, while ignorance is the root.
Therefore, dream-phenomena necessarily depend upon the state of sleep;
likewise, by contemplating ignorance, one directly perceives the true reality (*dharmatā*).
One merely observes that grasping at signs is but the perception of true reality.
If one were to distinguish this emptiness from that of the Two Vehicles,
then there would be the two vehicles of the two teachings, as well as the entry into emptiness through the Shared and Distinct [Teachings].
It can be understood spontaneously.
Even if the Separate Teaching (Pṛthagdharma) were to express non-emptiness,
why would it be necessary to engage in comparative judgment regarding what is not the contemplation of a beginner?
Therefore, it is in no way identical to the emptiness of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao).
Thus, this discussion concerns only the Two Vehicles and does not address the various other teachings,
as the meaning within this passage remains somewhat obscure and implicit.
Therefore, the subsequent text further clarifies this point.

As previously indicated in the section on "Correctly Demonstrating the Characteristics of the Gates," it first employs the three types of provisional designations (*prajñapti*) from the prior practice of Madhyamaka to distinguish the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, it is said as before:
since one employs the fourfold analysis to contemplate and shatter ignorance,
both types of emptiness are fully realized as being unattainable.
This is precisely the gate of emptiness, wherein the characteristics of the four gates are not perceived.
This constitutes the refutation of the provisional existence of continuity;
since even the nature of phenomena does not exist, how could there be ignorance?
Therefore, one does not distinguish between the differences of the four gates;
it is simply the gate of signlessness (*animitta*).
A "gate" is merely a phrase, which consists of four phrases; because there is both the real and the conditioned, there is the subject and the object.
Because there is subject and object, there is an agent;
now, because it is not a true condition, there is no agent—
this is the gate of non-action.
Although these three provisional designations are employed, in reality there is no sequence between them.
Since even in the preceding Teaching of the Shared Vehicle, emptiness is itself formlessness and the absence of volitional activity,
how much more so in the Perfect and Sublime [Teaching], where could any further sequential establishment exist?
Regarding the passage beginning with "The king and his ministers," it also possesses three meanings that differ from those previously mentioned.
Such is the case for these [passages].
It clarifies that the three gates are mutually identical.
Furthermore, beneath the four gates, it clarifies that each of the three liberations within every gate interpenetrates one another.
As follows, it again distinguishes the differences between types of emptiness by means of the teachings.
The initial formation constitutes a circular gate;
therefore, it is said that the intent of the three gates is not sequential.
Although [the text] speaks of "separately" below, it still allows that the Separate Teaching (biejiao) also takes the true reality (shixiang) as its object.
Because it follows a sequential order, it differs from the Perfect [Teaching].
Furthermore, as for its differences from the Separate [Teaching], it is already distinct from that; how much more so from the Treasury and the Shared [Teachings]?
One must first be able to recognize their differing characteristics before one can contemplate their commonality; therefore, I exhort all beings to understand them well.
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (Huayan) classifies [the teachings] according to the five flavors (*pañcarasa*).
The initial text specifically judges [the teachings] by means of the five flavors.
It clarifies that the four foundations of mindfulness are simply the contemplation of the aggregates;
when one reaches Nirvana, they become the five liberations.
Liberation is precisely the secret treasury. Since the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) occupy the beginning of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma),
the withering and flourishing of the twin trees further symbolize these foundations of mindfulness.
Therefore, we revert to using witheredness and flourishing as the criteria for judgment.
Although both meanings are present within the *Avataṃsaka*, the text primarily clarifies their distinction;
thus it is said that the four aspects of flourishing predominate.
Therefore, while the ten kinds of Brahma-conduct in the first dwelling fully clarify the distinct meanings,
although the first dwelling briefly clarifies the perfect meaning,
from the second dwelling up through the tenth ground, they mostly clarify the distinct meanings.
Although the two gates of the *Puxian xingbu* (Avataṃsaka) were expounded within the *Xiangzhong* (The Ten Stages),
the meaning of Samantabhadra is sparse across those various stages;
it is only in the "Entry into the Dharma Realm" chapter that Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra extensively clarify the perfect fusion [of these teachings].
Other teachers mostly clarify the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa).
Therefore, it is now said that [this teaching] predominantly emphasizes the four glories.
The Tripiṭaka master’s interpretation is easy to understand.
Although the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā texts contain the meaning of perfection throughout,
they are mostly intended to discipline bodhisattvas of dull faculties and those of the two vehicles; therefore,
in the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra, the śrāvakas are rebuked and the bodhisattvas are disparaged.
To contemplate the seat and yet withdraw in hesitation is to invite derision;
to hear of inconceivable matters while one's faculties are already ruined is like being blind upon seeing a Great Being manifest his transformations.
Only then will you believe that the Mahāyāna is profoundly deep;
only those bodhisattvas with great resolve can,
upon reaching the assembly of Prajñāpāramitā, be entrusted with its full task.
Therefore, the Buddha supplemented his teaching by expounding the two kinds of emptiness.
Thus, the intent of the teachings during the two periods was largely to harmonize the withered and lead them into flourishing,
enabling those of the Two Vehicles to gradually achieve both the universal and the particular.
Although their meaning has not yet been explicitly taught, their flourishing is already established.
When the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* arrives, all that is withered and flourishing enters into that which is neither withered nor flourishing;
only then are they fit to receive the prediction of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, following the Great Sūtra, we have already moved beyond what has been said,
stating that the manifestation of transformation at the Śāla Grove was sufficient.

Although the two sūtras share the same flavor and thus move beyond one another while remaining complementary, it is therefore judged that [the teaching] was for those of extremely dull faculties who arrived at the Twin Trees.
The Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā manifests both entry into the Exoteric and entry into the Esoteric;
therefore, it is said that "the Bodhisattva attains entry everywhere.
This already cites the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as meeting the finger that points toward the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Therefore, we know that the Lotus Sūtra is the primary essence of the *amṛta* (the finest cream).
This is why the sūtra uses the analogy of harvesting in autumn and storing for winter;
by the time of the *Nirvāṇa* Sūtra, it is merely like gathering what has been left behind.
Therefore, the ninth fascicle of the Great Sūtra states:
"For example, in the darkness of night, all construction work comes to a halt;
whatever remains unfinished [is left as it is]."
One must wait for the sun to become bright;
likewise, those who study the Mahāyāna must wait for the sun of unsurpassed Great Nirvāṇa.
This sutra transcends the world; like those fruits, it brings great benefit and peace and happiness to all.
It enables sentient beings to perceive the Tathāgata-nature.

Just as in the Lotus Sutra, eight thousand śrāvakas received their predictions of enlightenment, at which point they were like the harvest gathered in autumn and stored away for winter, with nothing further to be done.
The icchantikas perform no cultivation of any wholesome dharmas.
The eight thousand śrāvakas are the same as the eight thousand people mentioned in the "Chapter on Retention.
This is explained according to the manifestation of the five periods.
If we discuss the fundamental purport of the teaching, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* takes solely the "opening of the provisional to reveal the ultimate" as its primary doctrinal theme;
it is precisely for this reason that it alone is named "Wondrous.
Furthermore, it is said that the subsequent section concerning persons summarizes the core intended meaning that is being manifested.
This merely signifies that the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) has been completed.
Regarding what is called "the six persons and the Tathāgata," the twenty-eighth [fascicle] states:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what kind of bhikṣu is able to adorn the twin śāla trees?"
The Buddha mentions six individuals as well as the Tathāgata.
While the six individuals reside in the cause, the Tathāgata resides in the fruit;
both cause and fruit receive the name of "ornamentation."
The cause and effect, from beginning to end, are fully endowed with the four virtues;
because the signified meaning is thus revealed, it is called "adornment.
As for the six persons who constitute the cause:
The Sūtra says:
"If there is a bhikṣu who receives, maintains, reads, and recites the twelve divisions of the sūtras,
correctly establishing their words and phrases."
"In this way, a bhikṣu is truly able to adorn the twin śāla trees.
The Lion’s Roar said:
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught,"
The bhikṣu Ānanda is that very person.
One who has attained the pure divine eye refers to Aniruddha;
one who has few desires and is contented refers to Mahākāśyapa.
Practicing the conduct of emptiness without conflict refers to Subhūti;
being well-cultivated in supernormal powers refers to Maudgalyāyana;
attaining great wisdom refers to Śāriputra.
For each individual, it was as extensive as [the discourse given to] Ānanda.
Later, the person who cited the result said:
"If there is a bhikṣu who can say that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature..."
Having attained the Vajra-samādhi and being fully endowed with the four virtues and the eight masteries,
such a bhikṣu is most capable of adorning the twin śāla trees.
Thus he uttered a lion’s roar.
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught,
only the Tathāgata is able to adorn the twin śāla trees;
were he not there, they would not be magnificent.
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will remain here permanently.
The Buddha said,
"The nature of all dharmas is a non-abiding abiding."
What is meant by "requesting him to remain"?
Although the preceding six individuals were said to possess great learning up to great wisdom,
they must necessarily proclaim that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
Having already heard and received their predictions within the Lotus Sūtra, it is not that they are unable to speak;
rather, it is simply that they have not yet reached the level of those who have attained the fruit.
Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata is the most capable of providing adornment.
Both the person who is the cause and the person who is the fruit possess four virtues.
Because the person who is the cause has only just begun to enter [the path], it says "only the Buddha.
Since even the śrāvakas are thus, the following passage cites the inferior to illustrate the superior.
If one enters nirvana and achieves the five liberations,
the four applications of mindfulness are manifested as the secret treasury;
this secret treasury is none other than nirvana itself.
Nirvana is simply the liberation through the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness.
Once the contemplation of the five aggregates as the foundations of mindfulness is perfected, nirvana occurs in the interim;
this is precisely the attainment of the five liberations from within the five aggregates.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"From liberation from form up to liberation from consciousness,
they are not identical," and so forth.
Next, one binds the four mindfulnesses and liberation to form the three Buddha-natures.

These three Buddha-natures are neither identical to nor separate from the reckoned six dharmas; because they are not identical, yet not separate; because they are inherently complete as principle (*li*), yet are the original delusion. They are not [merely] so.
Regarding what are called the six dharmas,
they refer to the five aggregates and the self (ātman). Thus,
it is stated in the Great Sūtra, fascicle thirty:
The analogy of the blind men feeling the elephant is concluded.
To harmonize the analogy, it says:
"Or there may be those who say:"
Form is the Buddha-nature;
even down to saying that "I" am the Buddha-nature.
One should know that the Buddha-nature is neither identical to nor separate from those six dharmas.
Regarding the three Buddha-natures,
they follow the meaning of the third fascicle.
In the text on the Foundations of Mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna),
the direct cause is neither identical with nor separate from form (rūpa);
the revealing cause is neither identical with nor separate from consciousness (vijñāna).
The causal conditions are neither identical to nor separate from feeling, perception, mental formations, and the self.
One should know that these six dharmas are merely three causes;
therefore, these three causes are neither identical to nor separate from the five aggregates and so forth.
The five aggregates are transformed to form the four virtues (*caturguṇa*).
Regarding the three virtues and their three causes,
they are fully explained as in the end of the section on the three virtues in the third fascicle.
That [classification] comprised both the complete and the distinct;
now we deal only with the complete.
While they are largely the same, their minor differences each carry their own intended meaning.

In the previous two interpretations, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) were correlated with the three virtues (*triguṇa*) and the four virtues (*caturguṇa*).
Now, correlating them with the five aggregates while further adding the self (*puruṣa*),
it is placed among the four virtues and correlated only with the three causes (*trihetu*).
Therefore, there are slight similarities and differences between the opening and closing [sections].
Next, the "Aids to Counteraction" (pratipakṣa) which assist the opening will be explained.
First, regarding the clarification of the intent for its introduction:
First, one must delineate the essence of that which is assisted;
therefore, it is said to serve as the foundation for all samādhis.
Consequently, the four samādhis must necessarily rely upon the inconceivable three samādhis of the Perfect Teaching (Eṇkyō) as their basis.
These are the aforementioned six, which are termed "right practice" (samyak-pratipatti).
That right practice is not explicitly revealed is precisely due to the presence of prohibitions.
To explain according to their respective divisions:
Teaching samādhi is precisely teaching the foundation of all practices.
In the current text, this is addressed solely in terms of the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) samādhi as the foundation of all practices;
if one enters the section below, it will be explained in detail as the foundation of practice for the present text.
The sharpness of the faculties (*indriya*) below primarily restricts the faculties to exclude the auxiliary mental states;
among the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), three are unnecessary,
and only those with dull faculties who possess obstructions employ this antidote.
In the subsequent passage, it says, "merely focusing exclusively on the three liberations.
This means that by exclusively cultivating the aforementioned path-factors of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), one opens up the three liberations.
As for the phrase "starting from the first fruit," this serves as an illustration by way of comparison.
For a brief moment, the two fruits serve as roots that are sharp but obstructed;
furthermore, although mundane wisdom (*laukikajñāna*) that severs the fetters is not a supramundane root, it is nonetheless sharp.
This is also the limit of the "unrestricted" (asaṃvara).
Regarding the mention of "two lines":
the two fruits constitute one line.
Worldly knowledge constitutes one category.
Of these two categories, the first still involves afflictions regarding phenomena,
while the latter constitutes an obstruction to the realization of principle due to the absence of phenomena.
The meaning of destroying the obstacles of phenomena and principle should be treated with their respective remedies;
how much more so for those of dull faculties who, being obstructed by heavy [defilements], do not cultivate the remedies?
As for those in the third fruit, because their fetters of desire are exhausted, it is not said that they require treatment.
Although mundane wisdom (laukika-jñāna) may sever the afflictions of the lower eight stages,

because it still involves the conception of a self (ātma-grāha), it must still be remedied by the Path. Therefore, among the five meditations for cessation (pañca-nivaraṇa-pratipakṣa), those with excessive attachment to a self [require this].
Furthermore, it is still necessary to apply remedies by teaching the doctrine of the elements (dhātu).
According to this principle, only those with sharp faculties are exempt from obstruction; those with dull faculties are not exempt.
Furthermore, for those who have attained untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and exhausted the fetters of desire,
there is no need for antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
However, the first two fruits [of the path] counteract afflictions by taking principle (*li*) as their object.
This is called "treatment through application.
In reality, it is not the same as the characteristics of the treatment of ordinary beings.
One should know that there is no exclusion; rather, one simply focuses exclusively on the six factors mentioned above, such as the objects and so forth.
If there are obstructions such as dull faculties and so forth,
the path of remedy will not achieve concentration or stability; thus,

Fools do not understand that the five aggregates are an accumulation of past karma and afflictions;
they conceive of a self with respect to conditions.
Regarding their own bodies, they should employ the method of the elements (*dhātu*).
One observes various natures, various karmas, and various characteristics,
namely the six elements such as earth.
Of these, the earth element is moistened by water.
Yet they do not separate from one another.
That water element is supported by the earth element;
therefore, it does not flow away or disperse.
Because the fire element matures it, it does not decay;
because the wind element moves it, it attains growth;
and because the space element is empty, food can enter and exit.
Because there is the element of consciousness, there is volitional activity.
Because it arises from various conditions, one knows that there is no self.
Furthermore, one contemplates this body as being filled with impurities.
Just as scattered sand is blown away,
so too do formless phenomena continue in a succession of before and after.
One who contemplates in this way attains the seed of the liberation door of emptiness.
